title: The Hidden Switch — How I Stopped Hating Hard Work (And Started Craving It)

sections.label: Phase 1: The Warm Entry
sections.text:
I had the best three months of work in my life last year.

Not because I worked less. I actually — I mean I worked more. But it didn't feel like work. Which sounds like one of those things people say when they're trying to sell you something. But it's not that.

It was more like. I don't know. Like I'd been pushing a car uphill for years and someone finally told me there was an engine inside it the whole time.
sections.speaker_directions: Direct address, quiet confidence — not a pitch. Let the self-corrections ('I actually — I mean') read as genuine, not scripted.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: The 'engine inside it the whole time' line is the hook's plant of the recurring visual motif — deliver it as a held beat, not thrown away.

sections.label: Phase 2: The Honest Struggle
sections.text:
So here's what happened before that.

I was stuck. Like. Really stuck. I'd wake up. Set the alarm early. Tell myself tonight — tomorrow's different. Tomorrow I start the real work.

And then morning comes and. The blanket feels like concrete. The to-do list just — it sits there staring back at you. And you know you should work but something inside you just. Won't cooperate.

I thought I was lazy. That's what I told myself anyway. I'd say — okay you're just not disciplined enough. You need to push harder. Be tougher. All that stuff.

But here's the thing I didn't understand yet.

I wasn't lazy. I was just. Running on the wrong fuel.

There's two types of fuel your brain can use for motivation. And I'd been using the weaker one. The one that runs out.

It's like — okay imagine you've got this incredible race car. And you keep filling it with regular gas from the corner store. It works. It gets you moving. But it's not what the car was built for.

That's extrinsic motivation. Money. Praise. Status. Avoiding getting yelled at. All the stuff that comes from outside.

And here's the weird part about how your brain processes that stuff.

Your brain gets more excited about wanting the thing than actually getting the thing. It's like being a kid on Christmas Eve. The anticipation is — it's almost better than Christmas morning. Because Christmas morning you open the present and then. It's over.

Same thing happens with work rewards. You're chasing the promotion. Brain's lighting up. Dopamine everywhere. You get the promotion and. Three days later you're back to feeling flat.

So I kept doing this. Chasing the next thing. Thinking — okay when I hit this — [[PLACEHOLDER — replace: 'this next number, this next milestone, this is where it clicks.' And it never clicked. I'd hit it. Feel something for about a day. Maybe two. And then I was already looking for the next one.]]

[[PLACEHOLDER]] That's the loop. That was three years of my life, basically on repeat.
sections.speaker_directions: The self-diagnosis beats ('I thought I was lazy') should land harder than the explanatory beats — this is confession, not a lecture, until the fuel metaphor arrives. The [[PLACEHOLDER]] close should land flat and tired — this is the low point right before the turn.

sections.label: Phase 3: The Hidden Switch (PLACEHOLDER — not in source script)
sections.text:
[[PLACEHOLDER — entirely EvoLink-authored, replace with the real reveal]]

Then something changed. Not overnight. But something changed.

I started noticing — the days that didn't feel like work weren't the days I got praised, or paid more, or hit some number. They were the days I was just. Stuck into something. Curious about it. Actually cared how it turned out, apart from what it got me.

Turns out that's the second fuel. The one that was already built into the car. You don't add it from outside — you just stop starving it by only ever running on the other one.

Some people call it intrinsic motivation. I just call it — actually wanting to know the answer.

sections.label: Phase 4: Resolution (PLACEHOLDER — not in source script)
sections.text:
[[PLACEHOLDER — entirely EvoLink-authored, replace with the real closing]]

So that's the switch. Not a productivity hack. Not a new morning routine. Just — running on the fuel the thing was built for in the first place.

That's what those three months were. I wasn't pushing the car anymore. I turned the engine on.

If you're stuck right now, and it feels like discipline should be working and it's not — maybe it's not a discipline problem. Maybe you're just on the wrong fuel too.
